articles.title: Blazing like 10 billion suns: NASA’s Swift sees a wandering black hole devouring a star
articles.summary: NASA’s Swift Observatory observed a supermassive black hole ripping apart a star more than 30,000 light-years from the center of a distant galaxy. The extraordinary flare briefly outshone its entire host galaxy in ultraviolet light and revealed a black hole about a million times the Sun’s mass.
articles.content:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has observed a rare supermassive black hole far from the center of a distant galaxy as it tore apart and consumed a star. Astronomers describe it as an apparent "orphan" because it sits unusually far from the galactic core, where supermassive black holes are normally found. No previous event of this kind had been detected at such a great distance from a galaxy's center.

"We were looking for these star-shredding events as a way to find otherwise invisible supermassive black holes wandering away from the galactic cores where they usually reside," said Robert Stein, a research fellow at The University of Maryland, College Park and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "With this discovery, which is one of just a couple that have been confirmed so far, we've validated a new technique and can use it to hunt for more."

A paper describing the results, led by Stein, was published on July 27 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

A Star Shredded by a Hidden Black Hole

The discovery began with an exceptionally bright flare produced when a star wandered too close to a massive black hole and was ripped apart by its intense gravity. Astronomers call this type of event a tidal disruption event.

The black hole responsible has a mass roughly 1 million times that of the Sun. Its presence was first suspected in November 2025, when ZTF (Zwicky Transient Facility), a sky survey operated by the Palomar Observatory in Southern California, detected an unusual burst of light in a galaxy about 750 million light-years from Earth.

"Out of the half million flashes ZTF detects each night, our new artificial intelligence algorithm automatically recognized a flare that looked a lot like a tidal disruption event, despite its unusual location in the outskirts of a galaxy," Stein said.

For several months, the flare became brighter in ultraviolet light than the entire galaxy surrounding it. At its peak, it temporarily radiated with the brilliance of about 10 billion suns.

Swift Confirms the Extreme Cosmic Flare

Additional observatories examined the source after the initial ZTF detection. The SOAR (Southern Astrophysical Research) telescope in Chile studied its spectrum and found features consistent with a tidal disruption event.

Astronomers then turned to NASA's Swift Observatory, which can examine wavelengths that cannot be detected by telescopes on the ground. Swift's UVOT (Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope), for example, measured the flare's temperature at about 54,000 degrees Fahrenheit (30,000 degrees Celsius).

"The combination of all this data helped us rule out other explanations and confidently say it's a tidal disruption event, despite its strange location," said Jonathan Carney, a doctoral student at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, who took the first spectra that supported the flare's interpretation as a tidal disruption event.

Hidden Heavyweights at Galactic Centers

Nearly every galaxy in the universe appears to contain a supermassive black hole at its center. Roughly once every 100,000 years, a star in a given galaxy may stray close enough to one of these black holes to be torn apart in a tidal disruption event.

Although such events are extremely uncommon within an individual galaxy, astronomers monitor millions of galaxies in an effort to find them. Current surveys typically detect about 30 tidal disruption events across the universe each year.

Before 2024, every confirmed example had been found in a galactic core. That was partly because astronomers concentrated their searches there, since all known supermassive black holes had been located at galaxy centers. A tidal disruption event also requires a very massive black hole because the gravitational pull of lighter black holes isn't strong enough.

That assumption began to change when scientists detected signs of a star being destroyed 2,600 light-years from the center of its host galaxy. The discovery encouraged astronomers to expand their searches beyond galactic cores.

The newly identified event is even more extreme. It occurred more than 30,000 light-years from the center of its galaxy.

How Did the Black Hole Get There?

The black hole's unusual location raises a major question about its past.

"It must have originated in a galaxy's center, but not the one it's in the outskirts of now," Stein said. "We think the host galaxy's supermassive black hole is still at its core, but the one eating the star could have started off in a small galaxy that merged with the big one we see today."

Researchers have proposed two possible explanations.

In one scenario, three or more galaxies merged. Their central supermassive black holes may then have become locked in a gravitational struggle that launched the lightest black hole toward the edge of the combined galaxy.

Another possibility is that a dwarf galaxy is still in the process of merging with the larger system. As stars from the dwarf galaxy entered the larger galaxy, one of them may have passed too close to the dwarf galaxy's own supermassive black hole.

"Further discoveries could reveal the origin of this apparent 'orphan' black hole," Stein said. "The key science question we want to answer is: How common are wandering black holes?"

Swift Awaits an Orbit Boost

Astronomers may soon be able to answer that question by finding more displaced black holes.

"Pointed science observations with Swift's UVOT and XRT (X-Ray Telescope) instruments are temporarily suspended as the mission awaits an orbit boost, which is planned for this summer," said co-author S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator at NASA Goddard.

Swift's primary mission lasted from 2004 to 2006, but the spacecraft has continued observing the changing universe for more than 20 years. Atmospheric drag is now gradually pulling it closer to Earth. Raising Swift into a higher orbit could keep it operating for even longer.

"Once it resumes normal operations, Swift could continue searching for more examples of out-of-place black holes."

A New Search for Wandering Black Holes

In the years ahead, astronomers plan to apply the same detection method to observations from the newly operational Vera C. Rubin Observatory, jointly funded by the U.S. Department of Energy and National Science Foundation, in Chile and NASA's upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

"Rubin's wide, deep surveys will reveal a much larger sample of tidal disruption events than current observatories are capable of collecting, including ones that are off-center," Carney said. "And Roman's space-based surveys will extend the current search zone by seeing ones that are farther away, looking back through 9 billion years of cosmic history."

Combining data from Rubin, Roman, Swift, and ground-based observatories could allow scientists to identify many more wandering black holes. Together, these discoveries may eventually help astronomers build the most complete census yet of the universe's enormous black holes.

articles.personality_title: NASA spots rare black hole tearing apart a star far from galaxy center
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Most supermassive black holes are found at the centers of galaxies, where they quietly pull in gas and stars. Occasionally, a star gets too close and is torn apart in a bright event called a tidal disruption event. Until recently, all such events were seen near galaxy centers.

**What happened** – NASA’s Swift Observatory detected a supermassive black hole about a million times the Sun’s mass shredding a star more than 30,000 light-years from the center of its galaxy. This “wandering” black hole was spotted after the Zwicky Transient Facility noticed a sudden bright flash in ultraviolet light. The flare shone brighter than the entire galaxy for several months. Other telescopes confirmed this was a rare tidal disruption event far outside the usual galaxy core.

**Impact** – This is the first confirmed tidal disruption event so far from a galaxy’s center, showing that some supermassive black holes can roam away from their home galaxy’s core. It challenges the long-held idea that these giant black holes always stay put at the center. Discovering such “orphan” black holes helps scientists learn more about how galaxies grow and merge over time.

**What's next step** – Swift will resume observations soon after an orbit boost, allowing it to keep finding similar events. Astronomers will also use new powerful telescopes like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to search for more wandering black holes. These efforts could reveal how common these black holes are and how they move through space.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s discovery of a star-devouring black hole far from its galaxy’s center opens a new way to find hidden black holes wandering through space.
articles.personality_title_fr: La NASA observe un trou noir rare déchirant une étoile loin du centre galactique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La plupart des trous noirs supermassifs se trouvent au centre des galaxies, où ils attirent doucement le gaz et les étoiles. Parfois, une étoile s’approche trop près et est déchirée lors d’un événement lumineux appelé événement de perturbation de marée. Jusqu’à récemment, tous ces événements étaient observés près des centres galactiques.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’observatoire Swift de la NASA a détecté un trou noir supermassif, environ un million de fois plus massif que le Soleil, en train de déchirer une étoile à plus de 30 000 années-lumière du centre de sa galaxie. Ce trou noir « errant » a été repéré après qu’un flash lumineux ultraviolet a été observé par le Zwicky Transient Facility. L’éclat brillait plus que toute la galaxie pendant plusieurs mois. D’autres télescopes ont confirmé qu’il s’agissait d’un rare événement de perturbation de marée très éloigné du centre galactique.

**Impact** – C’est le premier événement confirmé de ce type si loin du centre d’une galaxie, montrant que certains trous noirs supermassifs peuvent s’éloigner de leur cœur galactique. Cela remet en question l’idée que ces géants restent toujours au centre. Découvrir ces trous noirs « orphelins » aide les scientifiques à mieux comprendre comment les galaxies grandissent et fusionnent.

**Prochaine étape** – Swift reprendra bientôt ses observations après une augmentation d’orbite, ce qui lui permettra de continuer à détecter ce type d’événements. Les astronomes utiliseront aussi de nouveaux télescopes puissants comme le Vera C. Rubin Observatory et le Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope pour chercher plus de trous noirs errants. Ces recherches pourraient révéler leur fréquence et leur déplacement dans l’espace.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La découverte par la NASA d’un trou noir dévorant une étoile loin du centre de sa galaxie ouvre une nouvelle voie pour trouver des trous noirs cachés errant dans l’espace.
articles.personality_title_es: La NASA detecta un raro agujero negro que destroza una estrella lejos del centro galáctico
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La mayoría de los agujeros negros supermasivos se encuentran en el centro de las galaxias, donde atraen lentamente gas y estrellas. De vez en cuando, una estrella se acerca demasiado y es destrozada en un evento brillante llamado evento de interrupción por marea. Hasta hace poco, todos estos eventos se veían cerca de los centros galácticos.

**Qué pasó** – El observatorio Swift de la NASA detectó un agujero negro supermasivo, con una masa aproximadamente un millón de veces la del Sol, destruyendo una estrella a más de 30,000 años luz del centro de su galaxia. Este agujero negro “errante” fue descubierto después de que el Zwicky Transient Facility notara un destello brillante en luz ultravioleta. El resplandor fue más brillante que toda la galaxia durante varios meses. Otros telescopios confirmaron que se trataba de un raro evento de interrupción por marea muy alejado del centro galáctico.

**Impacto** – Este es el primer evento confirmado de este tipo tan lejos del centro de una galaxia, mostrando que algunos agujeros negros supermasivos pueden alejarse del núcleo de su galaxia. Esto desafía la idea de que estos gigantes siempre se quedan en el centro. Descubrir estos agujeros negros “huérfanos” ayuda a los científicos a entender mejor cómo crecen y se fusionan las galaxias.

**Próximo paso** – Swift reanudará pronto las observaciones después de un aumento de órbita, permitiéndole seguir encontrando eventos similares. Los astrónomos también usarán nuevos telescopios potentes como el Vera C. Rubin Observatory y el Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope para buscar más agujeros negros errantes. Estos esfuerzos podrían revelar qué tan comunes son y cómo se mueven en el espacio.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El descubrimiento de la NASA de un agujero negro devorando una estrella lejos del centro de su galaxia abre una nueva forma de encontrar agujeros negros ocultos que vagan por el espacio.
